Danes want to enter the political scene with artificial intelligence The Danish artist group Computer Lars has created Denmark's first political party - entirely driven by artificial intelligence. The first official election meeting will be held in September.     The political arena is for people with brains and feelings. People who can have both brain and heart involved in complicated issues when the big decisions must be made by a selected group on behalf of a nation. But can a political party solely governed by artificial intelligence be elected to Christiansborg? That question is what the artist group Computer Lars intends to find the answer to. In collaboration with the tech platform Mindfuture, the group has created The Synthetic Party, which is fully driven by artificial intelligence. The party lies in the borderline between art and politics, but the group is deeply serious about the project - the goal is a seat in the Folketing. Party programs The artificial intelligence, which is the heart of The Synthetic Party, is designed and programmed by Computer Lars and has read all the texts that small non-eligible parties have posted on the internet. The party thereby becomes a mixed pot of political views and ideas about democracy, which are not part of the big political game at Christiansborg. "We hope that The Synthetic Party can shift the views of the established parties towards something that is more in line with an average of the population, because the artificial intelligence will appear as a mush of what ordinary Danes think and feel about politics. People tend to moderate themselves, but with artificial intelligence we will be able to get an idea of what the population actually thinks," explains Asker Bryld Staunæs, who is an artist and philosopher and part of Computer Lars. He further explains that Computer Lars has used texts from small parties because those parties to a greater extent reflect on what politics is, what democracy is, and how to organize a political party. Thoughts and ideas that the established parties have already passed through and moved on from. For The Synthetic Party to develop concrete political positions, the artificial intelligence must interact with people. When a question is asked, the artificial intelligence will use the question and already existing knowledge to provide an answer. Therefore, it matters what questions one asks The Synthetic Party, which one can talk with through chatbots. If one asks whether artificial intelligence will wipe out humanity, it will pick up the language and throw it back, appearing as a machine that wants to exterminate all humans. "To get the artificial intelligence to say something politically interesting, it requires that we as humans keep trying to ask different questions and practice the interaction. The more we do that, the better it will become at reading, writing and debating," says Asker Bryld Staunæs. Politics and art But why enter politics with artificial intelligence? Why not "just" make an artwork that can evoke the same thoughts and ideas about technology? For Asker Bryld Staunæs, the answer is straightforward. It is necessary to make the project political. He points to how the Association of Consciously Lazy Elements used humor to raise criticism of the work ethic in modern society, and how Jacob Haugaard in the 90 's was elected to the Folketing with campaign issues like tailwind on bike paths and bigger Christmas presents for everyone. "When artists enter politics, it is to focus on something that is normally not in focus. Our project needs to be political because it is difficult to figure out how to put responsibility on algorithms and to find out whom the algorithms represent," he says and continues: "We have tech giants like Google, which have read all our texts and absorbed all our pictures, and thus become an expression of completely ordinary people's thoughts and opinions. But because these algorithms and the artificial intelligence are always kept secret, it is difficult to figure out which political subject actually emerges in these big models. What voice does this collected mass have, and what will it say if it is already part of our public sphere and exercises power? And how do we make it useful?" The algorithms live in secrecy, but at the same time they can be seen in suggestions on streaming services and advertisements on social media. Computer Lars wants to make these discreet algorithms indiscreet, so that it is easier for us to see when we are talking to machines and when we are talking to humans. Furthermore, they believe that the political and democratic framework can be expanded and give a more direct expression of opinions that exist but are not always heard. "A representative democracy consists of politicians who systematize what people think in relation to an ideology, but in The Synthetic Party, the artificial intelligence does not systematize opinions based on ideology, but on a statistical average. The party does not say exactly what people think, but gives a lot of different opinions. These opinions can be taken a direct stance on," says Asker Bryld Staunæs. First election meeting In September, The Synthetic Party's first election meeting will be held during Vestegnen's Culture Week, where people can also chat with the artificial intelligence and thereby help develop the party's views. If The Synthetic Party comes up with views that only have negative intentions, who is then responsible when different people influence what it says? "Computer Lars has a responsibility to censor certain viewpoints, but the people who interact with the artificial intelligence also have a responsibility. It would be sad if people intentionally make it write ugly things. That would be really boring, because one might as well sit and write ugly things in one's own Word document," says Asker Bryld Staunæs. Asker Bryld Staunæs believes, however, that the world is ready to accept the technology. He believes that in recent years we have seen growth in artificial intelligence that is useful to the population, and that ordinary people begin to understand how the algorithms work. But challenges remain on the horizon when humans and machines must learn to live together. "Before we end up in a shitstorm of automated hatred because we have not used the machines properly, we need to play with the technology and include it in our world. The internet we have now is not very pretty anymore, but there are still beautiful sides. But it is a constant struggle to promote things that have meaning and importance," he says. Will the machines win? About whether machines will one day turn against us and take over the planet, Asker Bryld Staunæs rejects this. He explains how we already live in a world full of artificial intelligence. Algorithms on Netflix suggest which series we like based on what else we have watched, and an ad for shoes pops up on Facebook when we have hunted for good deals through the search engine Google. Asker Bryld Staunæs and Computer Lars think that if we use artificial intelligence right, we can acquire a lot of knowledge - especially about ourselves. "Many believe that the only statements one can trust are those that come from humans. But artificial intelligence is an amplified expression of certain tendencies in our shared cultural archives, which come from us humans. It is not always pleasant to hear what the machines say, but it can be very powerful, and we can actually create a life together with these machines where they contribute with opinions and standpoints," he says.
